# A message queue as an extension

[pgmq](https://github.com/pgmq/pgmq) is a message queue in the style of Amazon SQS, written as a
Postgres extension in plain SQL. A queue is a table, and every operation is a SQL function, such as
`pgmq.send`, `pgmq.read`, `pgmq.delete` and `pgmq.archive`. Because there is no client library and no
worker framework, anything that can run SQL can send or receive messages, from psql to a trigger
to a Go service.

## The visibility timeout

The idea behind pgmq is the **visibility timeout**. `read` does not mark a message as owned by a
consumer. Instead it moves the message's `vt` timestamp into the future, and until that moment no
other reader sees the message. A queue's whole life takes four calls:

```sql
SELECT pgmq.create('jobs');
SELECT pgmq.send('jobs', '{"page": "orm/quickstart"}');
SELECT msg_id, read_ct, message FROM pgmq.read('jobs', 30, 1);   -- hidden for 30 s
SELECT pgmq.archive('jobs', 1);                                  -- done: moved to pgmq.a_jobs
```

A consumer that finishes its work deletes or archives the message. A consumer that crashes does
nothing at all. When `vt` passes, the message is visible again, and its `read_ct` column counts
the new attempt. In the notebook, consumer A reads a message with a 2 second timeout and then dies.
Consumer B gets nothing at first, then gets the same message 2.2 seconds later with `read_ct` 2.

## At least once, and how to keep a lease

Delivery is therefore **at least once**, which means a message can reach more than one consumer. pgmq cannot
tell a slow consumer from a crashed one, so long work must call `set_vt` to extend its lease (the
time it keeps the message hidden). In the notebook, a 3 second job on a 2 second timeout loses its
message to a second consumer. The same job keeps the message when it extends the lease every half
second.

`pop` reads and deletes a message in one statement, which gives at-most-once delivery instead. A
message that a consumer pops and then fails on is gone.

## Retries from two columns

pgmq has no retry policy of its own. It has `read_ct` and `set_vt`, and those two are enough to
write one, as in this consumer loop:

```python
for msg_id, read_ct, message in read_batch():
    try:
        handle(message)
        archive(msg_id)
    except Exception:
        if read_ct >= 3:
            with conn.transaction():       # in exactly one of the two queues, always
                send("jobs_dead", message)
                delete("jobs", msg_id)
        else:
            set_vt(msg_id, 2 ** read_ct)  # backoff
```

The notebook runs this loop against a flaky page and a broken one. The flaky page succeeds on its
second attempt, and the broken one lands in the dead-letter queue after its third.

## What else it does

- **Many consumers.** `read` claims messages with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` inside one `UPDATE`.
  Four threads reading 400 messages took exactly 100 each, none twice, in 0.12 s.
- **Waking up.** `read_with_poll` waits for messages inside Postgres. `enable_notify_insert` adds a
  trigger that sends `NOTIFY` on `pgmq.q_<name>.INSERT`. From send to receipt, NOTIFY took about
  12 ms (median of 8), while polling took up to its interval.
- **Delayed messages.** `send(queue, msg, delay)` sets `vt` in the future when the message is
  inserted.
- **FIFO groups.** Messages with the same `x-pgmq-group` header come out of `read_grouped` in order,
  one at a time. A plain `read` on the same queue ignores groups, so every consumer of that queue
  has to use the grouped functions.
- **Topics.** `bind_topic('orders.*.paid', 'payments')` and `send_topic('orders.eu.paid', msg)`
  route messages with RabbitMQ-style wildcards. In a pattern, `*` matches one word and `#` matches
  any number of words after a dot.
- **Archive tables.** `pgmq.a_<name>` keeps every archived message with its `archived_at` time,
  which makes a free audit log.

## pgmq and pgqueuer side by side

Both claim work with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, and neither holds a lock while the work runs. They
differ in how a claim expires and in where the logic lives. In pgmq the claim is a timestamp that
the consumer must keep pushing forward. In pgqueuer it is a `picked` status, and the library keeps
the worker's heartbeat fresh for you.

| | pgmq | pgqueuer |
|---|---|---|
| what it is | a Postgres extension, SQL functions | a Python library over plain tables |
| a claim | `read` pushes `vt` ahead | dequeue sets `status = 'picked'` |
| a claim expires | when `vt` passes, unless the consumer calls `set_vt` | when the worker's heartbeat is older than `heartbeat_timeout`, refreshed for you |
| consumers | any language with a Postgres driver | Python asyncio workers |
| waking up | `read_with_poll`, or `enable_notify_insert` and `LISTEN` | `LISTEN ch_pgqueuer`, always on |
| retries | by hand, from `read_ct` and `set_vt` | built in, with `on_failure="hold"` |
| extras | archive, topics, FIFO groups, partitioned queues | dedupe keys, fleet-wide limits, cron schedules |

pgmq suits a queue that several languages or services share, or one fed from SQL itself, where an
SQS-shaped API is the point. pgqueuer suits a Python application that wants a worker framework with
retries, limits and schedules already written.

::: {.callout-note}
## In the lab

pgmq 1.13 has no Debian package for Postgres 18 yet, so `docker/Dockerfile.pg18` builds it from
source. It is plain SQL, installed with PGXS. The [pgmq playground](../notebooks/pgmq_playground.ipynb)
notebook runs every step above against that server.
